## Talk title

**Setting the legal limit with an R package: fifteen years of open-source software in
environmental regulation**

Alternatives, in roughly decreasing order of restraint:

- *From scripts on a hard drive to open-source regulatory infrastructure — and what changed
  when the AI arrived*
- *White, grey and black: open code, confidential data, and the numbers that stop an operation*
- *From SourceForge to statute: how an open-source R package ended up setting water quality
  limits in three countries*

---

## Abstract — primary version

Environmental regulation runs on numbers. A dredging campaign operates against turbidity
triggers that stop the vessel if they are exceeded; a discharge is licensed against a safe
concentration for each contaminant. Those numbers have to be defensible — to a regulator, to
a proponent, and occasionally in court — and increasingly they are produced by open-source R
packages.

I am a quantitative ecologist at the Australian Institute of Marine Science, with a sound
applied grasp of statistics and no formal training in programming. This talk traces fifteen
years of accidental software development, organised around a single question: how far could
the software travel?

**Era one produced scripts rather than software.** `ElicitN`, published in *Environmental
Modelling & Software* in 2012 with four co-authors, was 57 R scripts distributed as a zip
file. The statistics were novel; the tool was effectively unreproducible within five years.
None of the five of us thought to ask whether it would still run.

**Era two ran as two strands that never properly met.** One was industry monitoring data: a
large dredging campaign at Barrow Island, over 1,500 coral colonies scored fortnightly for 530
days, from which we derived *in situ* dose–response relationships and probabilistic thresholds
using ROC curves. Those numbers are still in regulatory use. The code behind them is bespoke,
entangled with data I cannot distribute, and has never been installable by anyone. The other
strand was GitHub and packaging — `FSSgam` and `epower` — built from data I *could* share, and
on which no regulation depends. The pattern is backwards: the higher the stakes, the less
shareable the tooling. I will argue that building open tools around confidential data is a
real and largely unsolved problem, and one worth more attention than it gets.

**Era three was CRAN.** `bayesnec` and `ssddata` were released in 2021, and CRAN submission
was the first time anything external held my code to a standard. Separately — and this matters
— a long track record in the field, and convening workshops with the people who set these
guidelines, led to a joint Australian–Canadian evaluation of `ssdtools` against the incumbent
closed-source tool, and its adoption as the default for deriving water quality guideline
values in Australia, New Zealand and Canada. Domain credibility got me into that room; the
software skills mattered once I was in it. Open source was not a convenience in that process:
it was the precondition for multi-jurisdictional agreement, because three regulators cannot
audit a black box.

The talk closes on the last few months. I stopped writing code by hand in June. Rather than
assert a productivity gain, I measured it across 1,340 of my own commits: tests tripled as a
share of the work, packaging and continuous integration rose fivefold, and source code fell.
I will show where the change actually is — it is not in the typing — and which parts of the
job it does not touch.

Two things I would like to leave the room with: that the unglamorous maintenance work which
determines whether research software outlives its project has just become very much cheaper
to do; and that we still have no good pattern for building open, reusable tooling on top of
data that cannot be shared.

*(537 words)*

---

## Abstract — short version

Environmental regulation runs on numbers: the turbidity trigger that stops a dredge, the
concentration limit written into a discharge licence. Increasingly, those numbers come out of
open-source R packages.

I am a quantitative ecologist with no formal training in programming who now maintains
software used to derive water quality guideline values in Australia, New Zealand and Canada.
This talk traces fifteen years of accidental software development in three eras — scripts,
GitHub, and CRAN — from a 2012 tool that was unreproducible within five years, through
`FSSgam` and `epower`, to `bayesnec`, `ssddata` and `ssdtools` and their adoption in
regulation. Alongside that runs a large body of confidential industry monitoring data which
produced numbers still in regulatory use and no shareable software at all — a gap I will argue
is real and largely unsolved.

It closes on the last few months. I stopped writing code by hand in June. Rather than assert
a productivity gain I measured it, across 1,340 of my own commits: tests tripled as a share of
the work, packaging and continuous integration rose fivefold, and source code fell. I will
show where the change actually is, and which parts of the job it does not touch.

*(200 words)*

> A quantitative ecologist with no programming training on fifteen years of building
> open-source R software for environmental regulation — and what her own commit history says
> actually changed when she stopped writing code by hand.

## Speaker biography

Rebecca Fisher is a quantitative ecologist at the Australian Institute of Marine Science,
with over 25 years of experience in marine ecology and more than 100 peer-reviewed papers
and technical reports. Her interests lie at the interface between ecology, numerical
modelling and quantitative decision science, and she is committed to environmental science
research that is of direct relevance to government and industry end users.

Her recent work focuses on statistical ecotoxicology, developing robust tools for
quantifying and handling uncertainty in environmental risk management. She is an author or
contributor to the R packages `ssdtools`, `bayesnec`, `epower`, `FSSgam` and `ElicitN`, and
co-led the joint Australian–Canadian investigation that resulted in `ssdtools` being adopted
as the default software for deriving water quality guideline values.

GitHub: [beckyfisher](https://github.com/beckyfisher) ·
[open-AIMS](https://github.com/open-AIMS)

*(140 words)*

## Submission notes

- **Event:** R Exchange Perth 2026, 14–15 October 2026, Perth CBD (Epi).
- **Suggested session:** Day two, session three — *real-life applications*.
- **Requested length:** the programme suggests 20 minutes. The deck now runs **23:55** in
  full, with 20-minute and 15-minute cuts specified in `notes/slide-outline.md`. **Worth
  asking the organisers for a 25–30 minute slot** — the two-strands material and the
  unsolved-tooling problem are what make this more than a personal-journey talk, and they are
  the first things a 20-minute cut has to compress.
- **Contact for submission:** events@epi.group — no formal call for abstracts or word limit
  was published at the time of writing, so a ~540-word version and a ~200-word version are
  provided. Send the short one if a limit is imposed; the long one otherwise, since the
  three-era structure needs the room to read as description rather than as a pitch.
- **AV:** standard laptop + HDMI. Slides are self-contained HTML (reveal.js); no internet
  required. A `.pptx` export with speaker notes is also built.
